tools.image-pixelate.faqs.0.question: What's the difference between mosaic and pixelate?
tools.image-pixelate.faqs.0.answer: They're essentially the same — both divide the image into color blocks. 'Mosaic' usually refers to large blocks (for covering details), while 'pixelate' refers to small blocks (for retro pixel art).
tools.image-pixelate.faqs.1.question: Can I use it to cover faces or private details?
tools.image-pixelate.faqs.1.answer: Yes. Set the block size large (32px or above) to cover faces, license plates, and other sensitive areas with color blocks.
tools.image-pixelate.faqs.2.question: How do I get a retro 8-bit style?
tools.image-pixelate.faqs.2.answer: Set the block size to 4–12px and keep the original colors — you'll get a pixel-art look like classic retro games.
tools.image-pixelate.faqs.3.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?

tools.image-oil-paint.title: Oil Paint
tools.image-oil-paint.description: Turn your photos into oil paintings. The algorithm counts the most frequent quantized color in each pixel neighborhood and paints with it, mimicking a painter's brushstrokes. Adjust the brush radius and color quantization level — all processing happens locally in your browser.
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.0.question: How does the oil paint effect work?
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.0.answer: The algorithm counts the most frequent quantized color in each pixel neighborhood and fills the center pixel with it, mimicking the smearing and blending of an oil painting brush.
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.1.question: What do radius and levels mean?
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.1.answer: Radius controls the brush size (larger means thicker strokes); levels control color quantization (fewer levels means simpler colors and a bolder style).
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.2.question: Which photos work best?
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.2.answer: Landscapes, still lifes, and portraits all work well. Photos with rich detail produce more vivid results — start with the default settings and adjust from there.
tools.image-oil-paint.faqs.3.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?

tools.image-edge-detect.faqs.0.question: How does edge detection work?
tools.image-edge-detect.faqs.0.answer: The tool uses the Sobel operator to compute the brightness gradient of each pixel in the horizontal and vertical directions. Pixels with large gradients are edges, and the result is a black-and-white line drawing.
tools.image-edge-detect.faqs.1.question: What does the threshold mean?
tools.image-edge-detect.faqs.1.answer: The threshold decides which gradients count as edges: lower thresholds detect more lines, while higher thresholds keep only the most obvious outlines.

tools.image-histogram.title: Image Histogram
tools.image-histogram.description: View the RGB channel and brightness histogram of your image to understand its exposure and color distribution. All analysis happens locally in your browser — your image is never uploaded.
tools.image-histogram.faqs.0.question: What is an image histogram?
tools.image-histogram.faqs.0.answer: A histogram counts how many pixels sit at each brightness level (0-255): the horizontal axis is brightness and the vertical axis is pixel count. It gives you an instant read on your image's exposure and contrast.
tools.image-histogram.faqs.1.question: How can I tell if my image is overexposed or underexposed?
tools.image-histogram.faqs.1.answer: If the histogram bunches up on the right side (near 255), the image is overexposed; if it bunches up on the left (near 0), it's underexposed. A well-exposed image usually has a fairly even spread.
tools.image-histogram.faqs.2.question: What's the difference between an RGB histogram and a brightness histogram?
tools.image-histogram.faqs.2.answer: An RGB histogram charts the red, green, and blue channels separately, while a brightness histogram combines them by how bright they appear to the human eye — making it better for judging overall exposure.
tools.image-histogram.faqs.3.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?
tools.image-histogram.faqs.3.answer: No. All analysis happens locally in your browser — your image never leaves your device.

tools.image-histogram.guide.whatIs.title: What Is an Image Histogram?
An image histogram charts how many pixels sit at each brightness level (0-255). The horizontal axis is brightness — dark on the left, bright on the right — and the vertical axis is the number of pixels at that brightness.

By reading the histogram you can quickly tell whether an image is properly exposed, whether its contrast is high or low, and whether the colors are shifted. It's one of the most common diagnostic tools in photography and design.
tools.image-histogram.guide.howTo.title: How to View an Image Histogram
tools.image-histogram.guide.howTo.intro: Three steps to view your image histogram:
Click the upload area and choose a local image (PNG, JPG, WEBP, or BMP supported).
The histogram is generated automatically as soon as the image loads.
Switch between RGB channels and brightness modes to inspect different dimensions of the color distribution.
tools.image-histogram.guide.tips.title: Tips
tools.image-histogram.guide.tips.items.0: If the histogram leans left, the image is dark; if it leans right, the image is bright.
tools.image-histogram.guide.tips.items.1: In RGB mode, the overlap of the three channels indicates color balance — a strong shift toward one channel means a color cast.
tools.image-histogram.guide.tips.items.2: If the histogram is pushed against both edges with a hollow middle, the image has very high contrast.

tools.image-palette.description: Automatically analyze the dominant colors in an image and generate a color palette. Choose between 4-16 colors and click any swatch to copy its HEX value. Everything runs locally in your browser.
tools.image-palette.faqs.0.question: How does color extraction work?
tools.image-palette.faqs.0.answer: The tool uses a median cut algorithm to analyze every pixel, group similar colors together, and average each group into one representative color — giving you the color combination that best represents the image.
tools.image-palette.faqs.1.question: Is more colors always better?
tools.image-palette.faqs.1.answer: Not necessarily. 4-8 colors are usually enough to capture an image's overall tone. More colors add more detail but can also produce near-duplicate shades, so pick based on the image's complexity.
tools.image-palette.faqs.2.question: What format are the extracted colors in?
tools.image-palette.faqs.2.answer: Every swatch shows its HEX value (e.g. #FF5733). Click a swatch to copy it in one click, ready to paste into your design tool.
tools.image-palette.faqs.3.question: Is my image uploaded anywhere?
tools.image-palette.faqs.3.answer: No. All analysis happens locally in your browser — your image never leaves your device.
